rules.text: Never use :latest tag in production. Pin to a specific version like node:20.11.0-alpine or a digest node@sha256:abc for reproducible, auditable builds.
Always add a .dockerignore file. Exclude .git, .env, node_modules, *.log to prevent secrets leaking into the image and reduce build context size.
Use multi-stage builds to separate build and runtime stages. Final image should contain only the compiled artifact and runtime dependencies — not build tools, compilers, or test frameworks.
Optimize layer caching: Copy dependency manifests first (package.json, requirements.txt), install dependencies, then copy source code. Code changes do not bust the dependency cache.
Use slim or alpine base images. node:20-alpine (~7MB) vs node:20 (~900MB). Smaller images mean faster pulls, less attack surface, and lower registry storage costs.
Chain RUN commands with && and clean up in the same layer: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* to prevent caching stale package lists.
Use COPY over ADD unless you specifically need ADD features (remote URL fetch or tar extraction). COPY is explicit and predictable.
Add HEALTHCHECK to every production image. Orchestrators use this to detect unhealthy containers and stop routing traffic to them.
Never run containers as root. Add USER node (or a non-root UID like USER 1000:1000) before CMD/ENTRYPOINT in every production Dockerfile.
Never store secrets in ENV instructions. ENV values are baked into the image and visible via docker inspect and docker history. Use Docker secrets, Vault, or runtime injection instead.
Scan images for CVEs before every deployment using Trivy, Docker Scout, or Snyk. Integrate scanning into your CI pipeline and fail the build on critical vulnerabilities.
Never expose the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) to containers unless absolutely necessary. It gives full Docker daemon control — effectively root access to the host.
Drop all Linux capabilities and add back only what the app needs: --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE. Default Docker capabilities include many that are rarely needed.
Use read-only filesystems: docker run --read-only prevents runtime modification. Add --tmpfs /tmp for write access to temp directories only.
Pin base image digests in critical production workloads: FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:abc123. Tags are mutable; digests are immutable content addresses.
Enable Docker Content Trust (DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1) to only pull and run signed images. Protects against supply chain attacks.
Use --no-new-privileges: --security-opt no-new-privileges:true prevents processes inside the container from gaining additional privileges via setuid/setgid binaries.
Never use --privileged unless absolutely required. It disables all security profiles and gives the container near-unrestricted host access. Use specific --cap-add and --device instead.
Use user-defined bridge networks instead of the default bridge. User-defined networks provide automatic DNS resolution by container/service name — the default bridge uses IP only.
Avoid --network host in production. It removes all network isolation. Prefer explicit port publishing (-p HOST:CONTAINER) for controlled exposure.
Only publish ports that need to be public. Use expose: in Compose for internal service-to-service communication; ports: only for services that need host access.
Isolate services with separate networks. Frontend should not be on the same network as your database. Use multiple networks to enforce least-privilege network access.
Use EXPOSE for documentation. Even though it does not publish ports, EXPOSE communicates intended ports to operators and tooling. Always include it in Dockerfiles.
Never store sensitive data in container layers. Container layers are part of the image and accessible to anyone who pulls it. Use volumes or external secrets management.
Use named volumes for persistent data, not anonymous volumes. Named volumes are easy to inspect, back up, and reference across containers.
Back up volumes regularly. Use the pattern: docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz /data.
Use tmpfs for sensitive in-memory data (tokens, session data) that should never hit disk: docker run --tmpfs /run/secrets:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=65536k.
Use --mount instead of -v for explicit, readable volume definitions. It fails fast on missing directories and makes options obvious.
Set appropriate file permissions on volume-mounted files. Containers running as non-root users need ownership set correctly, often via an entrypoint script with chown.
Never commit .env files to source control. Use .env.example with placeholder values. Add .env to .gitignore. Load secrets from a secrets manager at deploy time.
Use healthchecks with depends_on. depends_on alone only controls start order, not readiness. Add condition: service_healthy with a proper healthcheck: definition.
Set resource limits on every service: deploy: resources: limits: cpus: "0.5" memory: 512M. Prevents one misbehaving container from starving others.
Use override files for environment differences. Keep docker-compose.yaml as the base, docker-compose.override.yaml for local dev, docker-compose.prod.yaml for production.
Use profiles to group optional services (monitoring, debug tools) that should not run in production by default: profiles: [debug].
Specify explicit network names in compose. Default network names include the project directory prefix, which changes between environments and can cause confusion.
Use restart: unless-stopped for production services instead of restart: always. It respects intentional manual stops and avoids restart loops during maintenance.
Use BuildKit for all builds. Enable with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 or in daemon config. Provides parallel builds, improved caching, and secret support.
Cache dependencies in CI. Use --cache-from and --cache-to with a registry or local cache to avoid reinstalling packages on every pipeline run.
Use --no-install-recommends with apt-get to skip recommended but unnecessary packages. Reduces image size significantly: apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends pkg.
Set resource limits in production with --memory and --cpus. Unconstrained containers can starve other services on shared hosts.
Use production npm/pip install flags: npm ci --only=production, pip install --no-cache-dir. Avoids dev dependencies and build caches in the final image.
Tag images with semantic versions AND git SHAs in CI: myapp:1.2.3 and myapp:abc1234. Makes rollbacks and debugging trivial.
Use multi-platform builds with docker buildx to support linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Essential for M-chip Mac development and ARM cloud instances.
